target: Deep dive: merchant onboarding restricted-business classification at a PSP/acquirer (head of merchant risk as rule-making owner; versioned public policy list; structured accept/decline/MCC/list-entry outcomes; approvals of business models)

refuted.point: ROI logic: gross labour value of settlement capture is $40k to $75k per year at a 100,000-application PSP, supporting an ACV of $20k to $40k.
refuted.why: The deep dive's own arithmetic does not hold. Item (ii), $25k to $51k from making 1,500 to 3,000 L1 reviews deterministic, is 60 to 70 percent of the total and requires deciding without a human that a new application belongs to a settled class, which means determining what the business actually sells from its website and product description. That is category B, which the minimal_product section explicitly lists under WOULD NOT DO ('classify websites or infer what a business sells'). If the class-membership signal is instead taken from the onboarding tool's own classifier (Ballerine's merchant report already emits mcc, lineOfBusiness and a per-report allViolations list with typed ids such as PROHIBITED_CONTENT: packages/common/src/schemas/report-schema.ts lines 102-135 and services/workflows-service/src/business-report/dtos/business-report-metrics-dto.ts line 51, vendor open-source code, commit 4303cd3), then the deterministic step is an MCC or indicator rule that Ballerine's docs already support ('set a rule on an MCC code to auto-approve, auto-reject, or move to manual review', adding_rules_and_affect_workflows.md line 8, sourced). Either way (ii) is not value the ledger creates. Item (i) is also overstated: 40 to 80 classes x 4 re-escalations = 160 to 320 avoided escalations, but the whole H pool is 150 to 300 escalations including first instances; the avoidable re-escalations are 120 to 220 (150 minus 30, 300 minus 80), or $9k to $16.5k at $75, not $12k to $24k. Corrected gross labour value on the deep dive's own assumptions: roughly $9k to $17k per year, plus at most a small fraction of (ii), call it $10k to $30k (estimate). That supports an ACV in the $5k to $15k range at the deep dive's implied value-to-price ratio and an ARR ceiling in the low single-digit millions with low hundreds of buyers (estimate). H8 fails outright, not marginally.

refuted.point: Verdict kill criteria: 'continue only if categories 7 plus 8 exceed roughly 15 to 20 percent of escalations, the PSP runs at least low thousands of escalations per year, and the median settled class is matched by at least three later applications within twelve months'.
refuted.why: These thresholds are set below plausible customer economics, which the brief (section 10H) forbids. At the deep dive's own cost figures, 2,000 escalations x 20 percent x $75 = $30k per year is the entire H labour pool at stake at a PSP that just clears the threshold; that cannot support the $20k to $40k ACV the deep dive proposes at any customary value-to-price ratio, and the orchestrator's own position notes (my_position_notes.md, local file) set the continue bar at an addressable H labour pool above roughly $150k per year at the median target, which at $75 per escalation and 20 percent H requires about 10,000 escalations per year, roughly 100,000 manual reviews and about 670,000 applications per year on the deep dive's ratios (own arithmetic). Only top-tier PSPs reach that scale, and the deep dive itself says those firms build in-house. A threshold that a customer can pass while the product still loses money is a preservation threshold, not an economic one.

refuted.point: Stripe's public vocabulary is 'weak but real evidence that the rationale for an acceptability decision is not stored as a typed, reusable object' and that 'acceptability rationale is not typed externally' at the two largest PSPs.
refuted.why: For Adyen this is overstated. The Legal Entity Management v3 spec (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Adyen/adyen-openapi/main/json/LegalEntityService-v3.json, vendor API specification, verified this session) types every VerificationError with code, message, remediatingActions (code, message), subErrors and a five-value type enum: invalidInput, dataMissing, pendingStatus, rejected, dataReview. The deep dive's key-number entry omits type and subErrors. That is a typed taxonomy of why a capability is withheld, including a typed manual-review state (dataReview). It is typed by error class rather than by policy class, so it does not carry the interpretation the product would store, but the claim that rationale is untyped externally should be limited to Stripe (whose account_requirements_error carries only code, a free-text reason up to 5,000 characters, and requirement: spec3.json, verified). The evidentiary weight of the 'not typed' argument is smaller than presented and, more importantly, the external API vocabulary says nothing about internal tooling, as the deep dive itself concedes.

weakened.point: 'The owner holds rule-making power over the PSP's own list and onboarding rules' and 'card-network licensed acquirers and payfacs with an in-house underwriting team number in the low hundreds'.
weakened.why: The rule-making power exists only for principal-member acquirers and PSPs underwriting on their own licence. Payfacs and ISOs operate under a sponsor bank's or acquirer's underwriting standards and the network's brand-risk programs, and the deep dive concedes the head of merchant risk 'does not control the network's MCC treatment' [RECALL, unverified: sponsor-bank binding of payfac underwriting]. The very APIs the deep dive read are the platform interfaces where the platform does NOT underwrite: Stripe's product_description is 'used by Stripe for risk and underwriting purposes' (spec3.json, verified) and Adyen's capabilities are granted by Adyen ('Adyen has verified the information, but found reasons to not allow the capability', LEM v3, verified). Sub-merchant onboarding on those platforms is therefore settled by the PSP, not by the platform, so the platform population does not count as buyers with rule-making power. The buyer set with genuine rule-making power is a subset of the 'low hundreds' recall figure, and its largest members (Stripe, Adyen, Checkout, Worldpay, Fiserv, Global Payments, Nexi, Worldline) build in-house, as the deep dive states. Buyer count is unknown but smaller than stated.

weakened.point: 'Settlements are approvals of business models rather than adverse consumer decisions', presented as the workflow's advantage over the H4 constraint.
weakened.why: The executable artefact the deep dive relies on is a 'Prohibited and Restricted Businesses' list. By construction a list entry is a prohibition or a condition; an approval of a novel model needs no list entry because silence permits it. So the part of the settlement that becomes a public, versioned, executable rule is predominantly the decline or condition side, which is exactly where the deep dive's own caveats bite: GDPR Art. 22 on sole-trader declines in the EU and France, and US political pressure on declining lawful industries [RECALL, unverified for both]. Approval-side settlements ('sweepstakes with features X are not gambling') would live in internal underwriting guidance, not in the list, and their executable form is a routing rule ('do not flag indicator X for MCC Y'), which is again an onboarding-engine rule. The 'approvals' framing is right about the absence of adverse-decision law on the approve side but wrong that the approve side is where the versioned executable settlement lives.

weakened.point: Recurrence: 'coverage at the list-category level is probably high' and settled classes are re-escalated 3 to 5 times per year.
weakened.why: After a class is settled, the next application of that class is not an ambiguity case; it is a factual question of whether this merchant belongs to the class (B), which is what the stage-1 verifier already said: 'Once the restricted list is settled most cases are B/A' (payments-fraud-aml-kyc.json, verification.corrected_workflow_verdicts). Re-escalation of a settled class happens only when the list entry is badly drafted, and the owner's existing remedy is to redraft the entry, which they already do (versioned list, recall). The recurrence that would justify a ledger is recurrence of the interpretive question, not recurrence of class members, and nothing in the deep dive separates the two. The prior IPSA analogy (93 percent coverage at coarse class, 37 percent at fine class, prior_evidence.md, sourced from primary data in a different domain) points the same way: repetition is plentiful where owners already govern with bright lines and scarce where disputes arise.

weakened.point: 'No human-review mandate' listed as a penalty NOT triggered.
weakened.why: For precisely the verticals where classification ambiguity sits (gambling, adult, pharmacy, nutraceuticals, CBD, firearms), card-network brand-risk programs require per-merchant registration and due diligence by the acquirer regardless of how the PSP's own list treats the class [RECALL, unverified: Visa GBPP and Mastercard BRAM registration duties; usa.visa.com blocked this session]. Settling the class therefore does not remove a per-merchant human step for high-brand-risk merchants; it changes which queue they enter. The deep dive names these programs but does not draw the consequence. This is an H4-shaped constraint on the very subset of cases the product targets, and its weight is unknown because the network rules could not be fetched.

weakened.point: 'Consistency and audit value against network fines and MATCH risk' as part of the value case.
weakened.why: The audit expectations the deep dive cites are per relationship, not per class: AML examiners expect documented rationale per higher-risk relationship (deep dive's own H4 note), network registration is per merchant, and MATCH listing is per merchant. Ballerine already integrates the Mastercard merchant-screening (MATCH) lookup as a workflow plugin (packages/workflow-core/src/lib/plugins/external-plugin/mastercard-merchant-screening-plugin.ts, vendor open-source code, verified). The per-merchant rationale is a case note in the case manager (E and F content: reserves, caps, conditions), which the deep dive itself excludes as non-generalising. Class-level provenance has no identified external consumer; its audit value is an assertion without a source (structural reasoning, no data).

weakened.point: The review split (A 30-35, B 30-35, C 8-12, D 2-3, E 8-12, F 3-5, G 2-3, H 5-10 of manual reviews) and 'H is the highest of any workflow in the payments cluster'.
weakened.why: The split is labelled as own estimate and the only sourced input is the composition of Stripe's error enum, which cuts harder against H than the deep dive reports. Re-counting the 96 codes in spec3.json (verified this session): 30 verification_document_*, 17 invalid_url_*, 23 further verification_* identity, ownership, authority and tax-id mismatch codes (for example verification_directors_mismatch, verification_failed_tax_id_match, verification_missing_owners), 19 invalid_* format and address codes, 5 *_denylisted, 3 other (external_request, information_missing, unsupported_business_type). So 91 of 96 codes are missing evidence, identity or factual verification, or input format (A/B); 5 are already-settled per-entity or per-string denylists; 2 to 4 concern supportability. The taxonomy contains no code at all for a restricted-business category decision. The deep dive's 'about 30 document, 17 website, 5 denylist, 2 to 4 supportability' is accurate but omits the 23 identity codes that make the A/B dominance starker. The claim that H is highest in the cluster comes from the same verifier who called the 10 to 20 percent figure a guess with no data.

weakened.point: 'No reachable evidence of a system that stores the interpretation with provenance separately from the rule', used to define the product gap.
weakened.why: True as stated, but the reachable incumbent shows how small the gap is. Ballerine's workflows-service loads its risk rules from a Notion database whose schema is ID, Rule set (JSON), Domain, Indicator, Risk level (positive/moderate/high/critical), Base/Additional/Min/Max risk score (services/workflows-service/src/rule-engine/risk-rule.service.ts, vendor open-source code, verified), evaluated by a risk-rules plugin that emits indicators by domain (packages/workflow-core/src/lib/plugins/common-plugin/risk-rules-plugin.ts). Its Prisma schema carries a Policy model {name, version, tasks, rulesSets} and a versioned WorkflowDefinition (schema.prisma lines 228-261 and 347-353, verified). The interpretation therefore already lives as rows in a table next to the executable rule, without author, date, rationale or source case. Adding those four columns is a feature of the incumbent, which is the deep dive's own strong prior; the gap is real and its closure is trivial for whoever owns the table.

strengthened.point: All checkable key numbers are accurate.
strengthened.why: Re-verified this session against the primary files: Stripe account_requirements.disabled_reason is a 15-value enum including under_review, listed, rejected.listed, rejected.terms_of_service, rejected.fraud, rejected.other, requirements.pending_verification; capability disabled_reason is a 10-value enum including pending.review and rejected.unsupported_business; account_requirements_error.code has 96 values; product_description is 'Internal-only ... used by Stripe for risk and underwriting purposes' with maxLength 40000; mcc is a free string; company.structure has 23 values; business_type has 4 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stripe/openapi/master/openapi/spec3.json, vendor API specification). Adyen verificationStatus values pending/invalid/valid/rejected with the quoted 'rejected' definition, capabilities acceptTransactionInRestrictedIndustries plus Commercial and Consumer variants and useCardInRestrictedIndustries plus variants, industryCode example 4431A (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Adyen/adyen-openapi/main/json/LegalEntityService-v3.json). 981 MCC rows (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/greggles/mcc-codes/main/mcc_codes.csv, third-party open dataset). Ballerine at commit 4303cd3 (14 Oct 2025): the MCC auto-approve/auto-reject/manual-review sentence and the 0742 example, the 5499/5912, 7800/7801 and 5941 document gates in us/common/rules.ts, 128-entry industries.ts for both US and EU, Manual review actions Approve/Reject/Ask for all re-uploads, MERCHANT_REPORT_STATUSES including conditionally-approved, and the README 'undergoing a major rebuild and is not actively supported' sentence (vendor open-source code and docs). Minor note: Adyen's verificationStatus values are documented in a description string, not as a schema enum.

strengthened.point: Main bottleneck is missing data or factual classification (penalty 2).
strengthened.why: Stronger than the deep dive states. Of Stripe's 96 requirement error codes, 91 are document, website, identity, ownership, authority, tax-id or format defects (verified count above), and the vendor onboarding tool already automates the factual classification step that precedes any interpretation: Ballerine's merchant report schema emits mcc, mccDescription, lineOfBusiness and a typed allViolations list (id, name, riskLevel), with PROHIBITED_CONTENT as the documented example violation id (verified). The classification into named prohibited categories is a vendor output; what remains for a human is whether the classifier is right (B) and, rarely, whether the category should exist (H).

strengthened.point: Existing rules engines and onboarding tools already solve the executable part (penalty 3, H3/H6) and the result is a feature of the onboarding tool.
strengthened.why: Additional shipped evidence beyond the deep dive's: Ballerine versions its Policy and WorkflowDefinition objects and stores risk rules as a Domain/Indicator/Risk-level table in Notion (verified above); Ballerine ships a Mastercard merchant-screening (MATCH) plugin (verified); Adyen's Balance Platform v2 spec types MCC-based restrictions as transaction rules with a reason enum {compliance, fraud, internalPolicy, policy, system} and an MccsRestriction object with anyMatch/noneMatch operations, described as 'if your business has policies about the Merchant Category Codes (MCCs) allowed on a transaction, you can create a rule' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Adyen/adyen-openapi/main/json/BalancePlatformService-v2.json, vendor API specification, local copy deep/psp/adyen_bp.json; issuing side, not onboarding, but the same MCC-policy object pattern). Every reachable incumbent holds the MCC-conditioned executable rule; none needs a separate ledger to hold it.

strengthened.point: Evidence limitation: zero reachable data on queue volume, manual share, recurrence or cost.
strengthened.why: Confirmed and not repairable this session. Beyond the blocks the deep dive lists, the GitHub API through this proxy is repository-scoped for both code and repository search (api.github.com returns 'sessions are bound to their configured repositories'), and the MCP GitHub search tools return 503/502, so no scrape, mirror or dataset could be discovered. PyPI's iso18245 package (https://pypi.org/pypi/iso18245/json, open-source package metadata) confirms MCC lists exist with Stripe, USDA, Visa, Mastercard and Amex descriptions but carries no restricted-category or brand-risk flag. Every operational number in the deep dive remains an estimate or recall, and the correct posture is uncertainty, not a favourable prior.

missing: Any measurement of the interpretive residual: the deep dive never separates recurrence of the interpretive question from recurrence of class members; the base-rate experiment design must code post-settlement cases as B (class membership) unless the underwriter had to re-decide what the list line means.

Buyer population with rule-making power: how many acquirers and PSPs underwrite on their own licence versus payfacs and ISOs bound by sponsor or acquirer standards (structure recalled, counts unknown; Visa/Mastercard registries blocked).

Network per-merchant obligations for high-brand-risk verticals (Visa GBPP and Mastercard BRAM registration, due diligence, MATCH inquiry duties) and whether they force a human step per merchant after the class is settled (recall only; no primary text fetched).

Whether PSP restricted-business lists actually change in response to cases: a diff history of Stripe's, Adyen's or Mollie's list across versions would show settlement frequency and direction (add, remove, condition); all pages and web archives blocked.
Whether Stripe's, Adyen's or Checkout's internal underwriting tools store class-level rationale with authority and date (unknown; only external APIs read).
ECOA/Reg B applicability to merchant accounts in the US and the AI Act treatment of merchant acceptance for sole traders in the EU, both asserted from recall and unverified.

Value-per-decision evidence: cost of a mis-approved prohibited merchant (network assessment amounts, MATCH consequences) is recall only; the deep dive already concedes the mechanism does not prevent that error.

The deep dive's claim to be 'the best-shaped workflow found across the fifteen sweeps' is not reconciled with the orchestrator's position notes, which pick in-company customs classification as the wedge on access grounds; no cross-workflow comparison was made on the same criteria.

Cost figures: $50 and $100 per hour fully loaded, 20 and 45 minutes per review, 15 percent manual share and 10 percent escalation share are all unsourced assumptions; the brief requires cost per decision to come from customers, not analyst arithmetic.
corrected_verdict: Evidence against a standalone product; the workflow keeps the least-bad shape found in the payments cluster but fails the brief on economics using the deep dive's own numbers, and its data base is empty. Corrections: (1) once the L1-automation item, which depends on website classification the product disclaims or on MCC rules incumbents already ship, is removed and the re-escalation item is made consistent with the H pool, gross labour value at a 100,000-application PSP is roughly $10k to $30k per year (estimate), not $40k to $75k, so H8 fails outright rather than marginally; (2) the executable settlement in this workflow is predominantly a prohibition or condition on a public list, so the 'approvals' advantage over H4 is smaller than claimed, and network brand-risk programs keep a per-merchant human step for the very verticals where ambiguity sits [RECALL, unverified]; (3) the buyer set with rule-making power is a subset of the recalled 'low hundreds', because payfacs and platforms are underwritten by their PSP or sponsor, and the largest self-underwriting PSPs build in-house; (4) the reachable incumbent already holds the executable half in a versioned Policy object and a Domain/Indicator/Risk-level rules table, so the residual gap is four provenance columns, which is a feature. Every volume, share, recurrence and cost figure remains estimate or recall; no data could be added because GitHub search is unavailable through this proxy and every regulator, network, PSP and press host is blocked. Recommendation: do not fund a company on this workflow. Run the base-rate experiment only if a single PSP or acquirer offers its historical escalation log and dated list versions at near-zero cost, code post-settlement class-membership cases as B not H, and use economic kill thresholds: continue only if categories 7 plus 8 together exceed 20 percent of escalations at 10,000 or more escalations per year and the median settled interpretive question recurs at least ten times per year, which is the scale at which the H labour pool clears roughly $150k per year at the deep dive's own $75 per escalation. Expect it to fail, and expect any positive result to be delivered as a provenance feature of the onboarding case manager.
overall:
EVIDENCE LIMITATION, STATED FIRST: WebSearch was exhausted before this refutation; every regulator, card-network, PSP policy and press host is blocked by the egress proxy; the GitHub API through this proxy is repository-scoped, so code and repository search returned 'sessions are bound to their configured repositories' or 503/502 for every query; PyPI and npm were reachable but hold no restricted-business or brand-risk data. Nothing below adds an operational measurement; all volumes, shares and costs in the deep dive remain estimates or recall, and I could not replace them. What I could do was re-verify every checkable number against the primary artefacts (Stripe spec3.json, Adyen LEM v3 and Balance Platform v2 specs, greggles/mcc-codes, the Ballerine clone at commit 4303cd3) and audit the arithmetic and structure.

Numbers: every key-number claim that has a source checks out (15/10/96 Stripe enums, 30 document and 17 URL codes, 5 denylist, 23 company structures, 4 business types, Adyen capability names and 4431A, 981 MCC rows, all Ballerine quotes and the 128-entry pickers). The deep dive under-reports the A/B weight of the Stripe taxonomy by omitting 23 identity, ownership and tax-id verification codes; 91 of 96 codes are evidence, identity or format defects and none names a restricted-business decision. Adyen's VerificationError is more typed than reported (type enum invalidInput, dataMissing, pendingStatus, rejected, dataReview, plus subErrors), which slightly weakens the 'no typed rationale' argument.

Arithmetic: the ROI logic double-counts. The largest item, $25k to $51k from L1 reviews made deterministic, needs either automated determination of what a business sells, which the minimal product disclaims, or the onboarding tool's own MCC and violation classification, on which the tool already routes by rule (Ballerine docs, verified). The re-escalation item exceeds the H pool it is drawn from; consistent figures give $9k to $16.5k. Corrected gross value is about $10k to $30k per year at a 100,000-application PSP (estimate), which cannot carry the proposed $20k to $40k ACV. The verdict's continue-thresholds (15 to 20 percent H at low thousands of escalations) let a customer pass while the H labour pool is about $30k per year; the brief requires thresholds set by customer economics, and the orchestrator's own bar of roughly $150k per year implies about 10,000 escalations per year, a scale reached only by PSPs that build in-house.

Structure: the versioned executable settlement in this workflow is a 'prohibited and restricted' list entry, so it is mostly the decline or condition side, where the deep dive's own GDPR Art. 22 and debanking caveats apply [RECALL, unverified]; approvals need no list entry. Network brand-risk registration keeps a per-merchant human step for exactly the ambiguous verticals [RECALL, unverified]. Post-settlement cases are class-membership questions (B), as the stage-1 verifier already said, so 'recurrence' as measured by class members overstates recurrence of the interpretive question. The buyer set with rule-making power is smaller than the recalled 'low hundreds' because payfacs and platforms are underwritten by Stripe, Adyen or a sponsor, as the very APIs read in the deep dive show. The reachable incumbent already versions its Policy and WorkflowDefinition objects, stores risk rules as a Domain/Indicator/Risk-level table in Notion, and ships MATCH screening and typed prohibited-content violations; the residual gap is author, date, rationale and source-case columns on an existing table.

Net: the deep dive's verdict 'promising in shape, unproven in size, likely a feature' should be restated as evidence against a standalone product, with the base-rate experiment worth running only at near-zero cost, with B-not-H coding of post-settlement class members, and with economic kill thresholds (H above 20 percent of escalations at 10,000 or more escalations per year, median interpretive question recurring ten or more times per year). The expected outcome is a provenance feature inside the onboarding case manager, not a company.
